name: Alitretinoin

lead: Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a retinoid prescribed as capsules for severe long-term hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma skin lesions. The payoff is calmer, clearer-looking skin where those conditions have been visible.

It activates both main families of retinoid receptors, changing gene activity that controls skin-cell growth and immune signalling. Trials are in those skin diseases; no source reviewed tested it for cosmetic purposes.

paras: The oral form is prescribed for severe hand eczema that has not responded to potent topical corticosteroids, and the gel is applied to Kaposi's sarcoma lesions. Both are used under medical supervision.

Oral use can cause headache, raised blood lipids and dry skin and lips, and pregnancy is an absolute contraindication. The gel commonly causes local rash and pain. Both forms are prescription medicines.

angle.text: Alitretinoin is a prescription retinoid that acts on skin-cell receptors to calm severe chronic hand eczema (orally) and Kaposi's sarcoma lesions (as a gel), leaving clearer-looking skin. Its trials are in those conditions, not cosmetic use.

lead: Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a naturally occurring retinoid that activates both retinoic acid receptors and retinoid X receptors. It is marketed as a topical gel (Panretin) for skin lesions of AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma and as oral capsules (Toctino) for severe chronic hand eczema unresponsive to potent topical corticosteroids.[1][2] It was developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals.[1]

It is a prescription medicine for skin disease; no source examined it as a cosmetic. Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication for oral use, and common effects include headache and raised blood lipids.[1][2]

paras: The topical 0.1 percent gel was approved in the US in 1999 for cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma lesions, and the oral capsule was authorised in the UK and several EU states in 2008 for severe chronic hand eczema in adults.[1][2] UK guidance in 2009 limited use to severe cases unresponsive to potent topical corticosteroids and other options.[1] German guidelines on hand eczema address its place in treatment.[3]

Oral use commonly causes headache, raised triglycerides and cholesterol, lowered HDL, dry skin, cracked lips, hair loss and joint or muscle pain; rarer effects include benign intracranial hypertension.[1] Topical use causes rash, pain and itching at the site.[1] Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication and pregnancy prevention programmes apply where oral use is approved.[1][2] Mood effects, including depression, are listed with unknown frequency.[1]

Alitretinoin modulates gene transcription via RAR and RXR, and in hand eczema is described as reducing cytokine expression in keratinocytes and T-cell activation.[1] Oral absorption increases with food, and metabolism involves CYP enzymes such as CYP3A4.[1][2]

Alitretinoin was once thought to be the natural ligand of retinoid X receptors, but later work did not detect its natural production in animal tissue.[1] The EMA approved it in 2000 for Kaposi's sarcoma, and the UK granted oral prescribing for hand eczema on 8 September 2008.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial in severe chronic hand eczema refractory to topical corticosteroids tested 10 mg and 30 mg daily for up to 24 weeks.[4] An earlier randomised placebo-controlled trial in 319 patients with refractory chronic hand dermatitis compared several doses with placebo.[5] A retreatment study examined patients with relapsed chronic hand eczema.[6] A phase III vehicle-controlled study evaluated topical 0.1 percent gel in cutaneous AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma.[7] Registered trials include a 513-participant comparison of delgocitinib cream versus alitretinoin capsules, alitretinoin versus azathioprine in hand eczema, and small studies in cutaneous lupus and mucosal lichen planus.[8][9][10] Grokipedia reports response rates of roughly 27-48 percent in hand eczema trials.[2]

timeline.event: US approval of topical gel for Kaposi's sarcoma lesions.[1][2]
